title: Ohm's law and power
body: Ohm's law links voltage, current and resistance: V = I × R. On a fixed 9 V, a 10 Ω resistor lets through 100 times more current than a 1 kΩ one.
The power a resistor turns into heat is P = V × I. Put the two together and you get P = V² ÷ R, so across a fixed voltage the lower-value resistor gets far hotter.
In a series chain it's the other way round. The same current flows through each resistor, so P = I² × R and the larger value runs hotter.
Every resistor has a power rating, and 0.25 W is a common one for small resistors. Push past it and the resistor overheats and can fail.
realWorld: Circuit designers check each resistor's power against its rating, so nothing overheats when the device runs flat out.
sources: OpenStax College Physics 2e, §20.2 Ohm's Law: Resistance and Simple Circuits. https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/20-2-ohms-law-resistance-and-simple-circuits
